label: Calculating with Conics
notes: This chapter, printed pages 189 through 208, turns the conic from a static quadratic curve into a computable projective object. Everything reduces to one symmetric matrix and the operations we can run on it: evaluation, the five-point fit, pencils, degeneracy, and intersection. Preview the journey from matrix to working toolkit.

label: Conic as a Matrix
notes: Anchor the algebra. A conic is the zero set of a quadratic form, encoded by a symmetric three-by-three matrix A. Points and lines are homogeneous vectors. Stress that scaling A or scaling a point leaves the equation invariant, so the conic is really a point in projective matrix space.

label: The Conic Through Five Points
notes: Five points in general position fix a conic uniquely. Each incidence is one linear equation in the six independent matrix entries, so five equations leave a one-dimensional kernel. Emphasize that the homogeneity removes the sixth degree of freedom, and that general position rules out three collinear points.

label: Bracket Determinant Formula
notes: Show the closed form. Instead of solving the linear system, expand a six-by-six determinant whose vanishing forces the running point x onto the conic through the five data points. The bracket form is coordinate-free and connects directly to the cross-ratio characterization of conics from earlier chapters.

label: Poles, Polars, Tangents
notes: The matrix does more than test membership. Multiplying a point by A produces its polar line; for a point on the conic that polar is the tangent. Pole and polar are dual through A inverse. Mention that polarity is the projective engine behind tangent constructions and conjugate points.

label: Pencils of Conics
notes: Introduce the pencil: every linear combination lambda C1 plus mu C2 is again a conic, and all of them pass through the four common base points of C1 and C2. Stress that one real parameter sweeps an entire family, and that the four base points are exactly the intersection of the two generators.

label: Degenerate Members
notes: A pencil generically contains three degenerate members, each a pair of lines joining the four base points in one of the three pairings. They are found where the determinant of lambda C1 plus mu C2 vanishes, a homogeneous cubic in lambda and mu. These line-pairs are the workhorses of intersection.

label: Intersecting Two Conics
notes: Here is the central algorithm. To intersect two conics, build their pencil, solve the determinant cubic for a degenerate member, split that member into two lines, and intersect each line with one original conic. The hard conic-conic problem collapses into easy conic-line solves. Walk the pipeline slowly.

label: Intersecting Conic and Line
notes: Explain the primitive that the pencil method reduces to. Restricting the quadratic form to a parametrized line gives a quadratic in one parameter; its discriminant decides two real points, one tangent double point, or a conjugate complex pair. The dual splitting via the skew matrix gives the same two points.

label: Tangent Constraints via Pencils
notes: Tangency is a limiting incidence: two intersection points merging. Using a pencil through given points, we can demand the conic touch a chosen line by forcing the line-restricted discriminant to vanish. This builds the conic through points with prescribed tangents, the four-points-and-a-tangent construction.

label: Complex Roots, Real Geometry
notes: Reassure students that complex roots are not failures. When a real line misses a real conic the two intersections are conjugate complex points, yet their join is a real line once the shared complex scalar is removed. Real projective computation must carry complex intermediate values honestly.

label: The Computational Toolkit
notes: Synthesize. One symmetric matrix supports membership, the five-point fit, polarity and tangents, pencils, degeneracy tests, and intersection. The recurring design pattern is reduction: manufacture a degenerate object whose split turns a hard problem into a primitive you already solved. Send students to the notebook to run each operation.
